additions.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 13: Transparency and provision of information to deployers
additions.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
additions.locator: Art. 13(1); see also 13(2)-(3) on instructions for use
additions.quote: their operation is sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret a system's output and use it appropriately
additions.why: The binding EU design-stage rule: a high-risk system must be built so the organisation deploying it can interpret its output, and must come with instructions for use. The Commission's copy of the consolidated text (stated as at 27 July 2026), not the Official Journal. EU law: it matters to UK firms only so far as the Act applies to them; no application date is given here.

additions.title: Data protection audit framework, Artificial intelligence toolkit: Contracts and third parties
additions.locator: Control measure 'Before procuring AI systems, datasets or coding, there has been appropriate due diligence...', list 'Ways to meet our expectations'
additions.quote: Choose AI models that offer transparency and explainability.
additions.why: What the regulator's auditors look for before a purchase: due diligence, explainable models chosen, and performance terms written into supplier contracts. Carries the 'under review' banner following the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025; the page shows no publication date, so the year is the year read. Data protection only.

additions.title: SS1/23 Model risk management principles for banks
additions.publisher: Bank of England, Prudential Regulation Authority
additions.locator: Principle 3.5 'Model development documentation', point (a), PDF p.24; see also Principle 2.6 on vendor models
additions.quote: Firms should ensure the level of detail in the documentation of third-party vendor models is sufficient to validate the firm's use of the model.
additions.why: A supervisory expectation that documentation for a bought-in model must be good enough for the buyer to validate its own use, and kept up to date. Sector-specific: addressed to banks, building societies and PRA-designated investment firms with internal model approval; covers all models, not only AI.

additions.title: Artificial intelligence in UK financial services - 2024
additions.publisher: Bank of England and Financial Conduct Authority
additions.locator: Executive summary, 'Understanding of AI systems' and 'Third-party exposure'
additions.quote: This is largely due to the use of third-party models where respondent firms noted a lack of complete understanding compared to models developed internally.
additions.why: Regulators' survey evidence that bought-in models are where firms' understanding is weakest: 46% reported only partial understanding of the AI they use, and a third of use cases were third-party implementations. Financial services only; a survey of regulated firms, self-reported.

additions.title: Artificial Intelligence Playbook for the UK Government
additions.locator: Section 'Transparency and explainability' (under using AI safely and responsibly)
additions.quote: Transparency can be limited by proprietary and 'black box' commercial tools
additions.why: Government's own guidance says explainability depends on the technology chosen and must be considered at design, and names proprietary commercial tools as the usual limit. Written for civil servants and public bodies; guidance, not a binding rule for companies.

additions.title: Commentary: Model Contractual Clauses for the public procurement of AI (MCC-AI)
additions.publisher: European Commission, Public Buyers Community (Community of Practice on Public Procurement of AI)
additions.locator: Section 1 (Background), PDF p.3; Article 14 commentary, PDF pp.11-12
additions.quote: an obligation on the Supplier to cooperate in explaining, at an individual level, how the AI system reached such an outcome or decision
additions.why: A worked example of a contractual explainability obligation: model clauses that bind the supplier to help explain individual decisions (clause 14, aligned with Article 86 of the EU AI Act). Voluntary templates drafted for EU public bodies, not UK law and not written for private buyers; the PDF carries no dateline (the year is from the publisher's file path and its resource page).

additions.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), NIST AI 100-1
additions.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
additions.locator: Section 3.5 'Explainable and Interpretable', p.16 (PDF p.21); Table 3, MEASURE 2.9; Table 1, GOVERN 6
additions.quote: Risk from lack of explainability may be managed by describing how AI systems function
additions.why: A widely cited US risk framework treats explainability as a characteristic to be designed, measured and documented, and third-party systems as a governed risk. Voluntary and from the United States; it sets no procurement or contract terms.

additions.title: Model Artificial Intelligence Governance Framework, Second Edition
additions.publisher: Info-communications Media Development Authority and Personal Data Protection Commission, Singapore
additions.locator: Section 3 'Operations management', 'Explainability', paras 3.26 onwards, PDF p.45
additions.quote: the organisation can consider requesting assistance from the AI solution provider as they may be better placed to explain how the solution functions
additions.why: International comparator: Singapore's model framework also places explanation on the deploying organisation and points it back to the supplier where the system was bought. Voluntary, non-UK, and softer than the UK regulator's position ("can consider").

additions.title: Stop Explaining Black Box Machine Learning Models for High Stakes Decisions and Use Interpretable Models Instead
additions.publisher: Cynthia Rudin (arXiv; published in Nature Machine Intelligence, 2019)
additions.quote: There is a way forward -- it is to design models that are inherently interpretable.
additions.why: The best-known research argument for settling explainability when the model is chosen: explaining an opaque model afterwards, the author says, is likely to perpetuate bad practice. Author's pre-publication version (v3, 22 September 2019) of a 2019 Nature Machine Intelligence article; a position paper, not an empirical study.

additions.title: Model Cards for Model Reporting
additions.publisher: Margaret Mitchell and others (arXiv; published in Proceedings of FAT* 2019)
additions.quote: we recommend that released models be accompanied by documentation detailing their performance characteristics
additions.why: The origin of the standard supplier document a buyer can ask for: intended use, evaluation across groups and limits. Authors' repository copy of a conference paper (FAT* 2019); a proposal with two worked examples, not evidence of effect.

additions.title: The 2024 Foundation Model Transparency Index
additions.publisher: Rishi Bommasani and others, Stanford Center for Research on Foundation Models (arXiv)
additions.quote: We find that developers now score 58 out of 100 on average, a 21 point improvement over FMTI 2023.
additions.why: Evidence on how much the large model suppliers disclose: 14 developers scored against 100 indicators averaged 58, up from 37. Shows why documentation has to be asked for, and that asking produces it. Preprint (v2, 4 March 2025); scores rest partly on developers' own reports; covers general-purpose model developers, not every AI vendor.

https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-.quote: the primary responsibility for ensuring that the AI system you use is capable of producing an appropriate explanation for the decision recipient
Selecting an appropriate model is important whether you are procuring a model from an external vendor, or looking to build a bespoke system in-house.

https://www.legislation.gov.uk/eur/2016/.quote: both at the time of the determination of the means for processing and at the time of the processing itself
enable the data subject to obtain human intervention on the part of the controller in relation to such decisions

https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-.quote: You are also required to specify your requirements at the procurement stage, rather than addressing trade-offs afterwards.

https://www.gov.uk/government/publicatio.quote: Encourage explainability and interpretability of algorithms and make this one of your design criteria.

rejected.title: CJEU, Case C-203/22 Dun & Bradstreet Austria (judgment of 27 February 2025)
rejected.reason: Blocked: the Court's site returned a four-character body to a plain request and the EUR-Lex/Publications Office address by CELEX number returned 404. Not read, not cited; no third-party copy used.

rejected.title: ISO/IEC TS 6254:2025, Objectives and approaches for explainability and interpretability of ML models and AI systems
rejected.reason: Blocked: iso.org returned HTTP 403 with a JavaScript challenge. Not bypassed; the standard itself is sold.

rejected.title: PPN 017: Improving transparency of AI use in procurement
rejected.reason: Read. It is about suppliers declaring their use of AI in bids and services, not about explainability of the system bought. Used for 4.6 instead.

rejected.title: NISTIR 8312, Four Principles of Explainable Artificial Intelligence
rejected.reason: Opened (reachable). Already logged in D4 as saying nothing on procurement; the NIST AI RMF covers the same ground with a third-party category, so this would be padding.

brief_check: Nothing read contradicts the approved brief. One dating point: the Commission's copy of EU AI Act Article 13 now says it is based on the consolidated text as at 27 July 2026 and no longer shows the 'not yet updated' notice the D4 log recorded, so the reason the brief gave for making no EU claim has lapsed (the brief itself is still accurate).
